newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Coffee growers govern in Nicaragua.
newsitem.headline: Coffee growers govern in Nicaragua.

text.p: When Nicaragua's new President Arnoldo Aleman looks out the window of his home and sees coffee trees, and this country's embattled coffee growers hope he will think of coffee as well.
Aleman, who took power on January 10, is a 51-year-old lawyer and coffee grower who lives on his El Crucero coffee farm outside of Managua, one of his three coffee farms.

He has named fellow coffee-grower David Robleto, the former head of the Nicaraguan Union of Coffee Growers (Unicafe), as Minister of Foreign Cooperation, a powerful cabinet post in foreign aid-dependent Nicaragua.
With coffee pundits in the top rungs of power in impoverished Nicaragua, its coffee growers hope this will be the government that will give them what they need.

"The fact that the president is a coffee grower, and knows the problems of coffee growers, and the minister of foreign cooperation is a coffee grower, is a reason to be optimistic, but we're going to wait to see it in practice," Unicafe's new president Amilcar Navarro told Reuters.

While the new government, which took power on January 10, has not yet released its official coffee policy, growers are encouraged by Aleman's promise to make agriculture his government's top economic priority.
In his inauguration speech Aleman promised to make Nicaragua, physically the largest country in Central America, "the breadbasket of Central America," as it was in the 1960s.
"We are a very agricultural country. The basis of Nicaragua's economic take-off will be its agriculture, and coffee is our main export," Aleman said.
Unicafe says coffee represents 25 percent of Nicaragua's exports.
Still leery of what they see as neglect by past governments, Nicaragua's coffee growers are guarded but optimistic.
"In conversations we have had with members of his cabinet we believe there will be a different policy towards the coffee sector," Navarro said.

Among Nicaraguan coffee growers' complaints are a lack of credit to finance production, a deteriorated infrastructure, a growing problem with "la roya" coffee rust, and rural insecurity as armed gangs in the lawless countryside kidnap, rob and at times kill coffee farmers, Navarro said.
Roads in coffee-growing regions are so deteriorated - often impassable - that Amilcar said it raised transportation costs by 10 percent.
Meanwhile, Nicaragua's main port, Corinto, is so expensive that most Nicaraguan coffee is exported through neighboring Honduras or Costa Rica.

These problems, accompanied by a cold snap in December and early January, have caused Unicafe to lower its projections for the 1996/1997 coffee harvest from 1,215,867 quintales (100-lb bags) to one million quintales. It projected exports to be 850,000 quintales for the harvest.

To ease these problems, Aleman has promised to rebuild the country's infrastructure and have its state banks provide credit to small and medium-sized farmers, who currently have no access to financing.

Aleman also promised to resolve Nicaragua's private property problem, a legacy of the 1979-1990 left-wing Sandinista government, which confiscated vast tracts of farm land, redistributing it as part of its agrarian reform.
"This is going to bring stability if the government fulfills what it has promised. It is going to help coffee production," he said.
